title: Al-Farabi, the second teacher
hook: the second teacher after Aristotle, on the virtuous city

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Sina: a cheap book from the market that opened a closed door, and the Canon, one ordered book of the body. Your line was: the canon.

That cheap little book Ibn Sina bought in the market had an author. He was a quiet scholar who, the stories say, cared little for money or fine clothes, and could play music well enough to move a room. Aristotle, the great Greek, was called the first teacher; later generations called this man the second teacher. His name was Abu Nasr al-Farabi, and the question he kept coming back to is still asked in town councils and in group chats about where to live: what makes a city good?
screen: `THE AUTHOR OF THE CHEAP BOOK.` → `THE SECOND TEACHER.` → `WHAT MAKES A CITY GOOD?`

segments.voice: Al-Farabi wrote a book usually called the opinions of the people of the virtuous city, al-madina al-fadila. His answer starts with a simple observation: nobody can live well alone. People need one another, so they gather into villages, towns and cities. But gathering isn't enough. What matters is what the city is for. The virtuous city, al-Farabi says, is the one whose people cooperate to reach true happiness, which for him means a life of knowledge and goodness, in this world and beyond it. He pictures that city like a healthy body: every part has its work, every part helps the others, and the whole lives well when each does its share. Then he describes cities that miss the point. A city whose aim is only wealth. Only pleasure, or honor, or ruling over others. Their people may be busy, even rich, but they have mistaken the road for the destination. And who should lead the good city? Al-Farabi pictures a ruler who is wise, truthful, just, and loves learning, like a heart that keeps the body alive. In his own account, this first ruler is both a philosopher, reaching the truth through reason, and a prophet, who brings it to people in words and images they can live by. Readers still argue over how he meant the two to fit. Either way, his test is plain. The city's walls aren't what make it good. Its aim is.
screen: `NOBODY LIVES WELL ALONE.` · `A CITY AIMED AT HAPPINESS.` · `CITIES THAT MISS THE POINT.` · `A RULER LIKE A HEART.` · then, large: `THE VIRTUOUS CITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the place where you live, your street, your town, your building, and ask al-Farabi's question: what is this place for? Picture it at its best: who would be looked after who isn't now, and which part of the body could you be, the hands that help, the eyes that notice, the voice that speaks up? If you pray, you can pray for the place you live and the people in it; if not, just hold them in mind.
Al-Farabi. The scholar called the second teacher, after Aristotle, who wrote that a city is good when its people work together toward true happiness. Today's word.
Your line: the virtuous city. Nobody, the second teacher says, lives well alone. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Students of Islamic philosophy read al-Farabi's book on the virtuous city as a picture of a community that cooperates toward knowledge, goodness and happiness.

chat.says: So what did al-Farabi think makes a city good?

Strong walls and wealth, so its people are safe and rich.
A ruler powerful enough that nobody dares to disagree.
chat.meaning: For al-Farabi, a city is good when its people cooperate toward true happiness. The walls aren't what make it good; its aim is.
